As of 210 AM Wednesday... 

KEY MESSAGE 1... Another above normal day today, followed by a 
mostly dry cold frontal passage on Thursday

Ahead of Thursday's cold frontal passage, this afternoon should be 
another above normal day as pre-frontal southerly winds usher warm 
air into the region. Maximum temperatures this afternoon look to be 
similar to Tuesday's, with highs expected in the lower 70s north, to 
the mid/upper 70s south. 

The cold front appears to move through the region Thursday afternoon 
into the evening. The chance for pre-frontal showers continues to 
trend down, with most models suggesting that most of the rain will 
dry up as the front crosses the mountains. Some very light rain may 
still be possible early Thursday morning ahead of the front, mainly 
in the Triad, and Thursday afternoon in the north. The REFS is 
suggesting that only up to trace amounts of rain are likely, with a 
lesser chance of 0.01-0.02 inches in a few locations. 


KEY MESSAGE 2... The chilliest air of the season will arrive and 
support the first widespread frost/freeze risk this weekend, 
followed by continued below average temperatures and dry conditions 
that will persist through most of next week.

A mid/upr-level cyclone will develop along the srn ON/QC border and 
lwr Great Lakes by Fri, then progress slowly across and offshore the 
Northeast and Atlantic Canada through the weekend, during which time 
a series of shortwave perturbations will progress through the 
associated cyclonic flow across and offshore the Middle Atlantic.

At the surface, a cold front trailing a deepening/redeveloping 
clipper low will have moved across cntl NC on Thu, with following 
cold and dry air advection that will initiate a step down to below 
average temperatures for Friday. A following, reinforcing cold front 
will slow as it encounters the srn Appalachians Thu night-early Fri, 
then move across cntl NC later Fri-early Fri night. High pressure 
will follow and build from central Canada to the Middle Atlantic 
this weekend through early next week, where it will remain while 
gradually weakening/modifying through most of next week.  

As temperatures aloft cool beneath the aforementioned cyclone and 
shortwave perturbations, a shallow layer of scant instability at the 
top of adeeply-mixed boundary layer may accompany the reinforcing 
cold front across cntl NC late Fri-early Fri night. Point forecast 
soundings indicate that buoyancy will coincide with a similarly 
shallow, 3-4 thousand ft deep saturated layer centered around 800 mb 
that will extend to near minus 8-10C, such that mixed phase clouds 
and precipitation production may result. While the aforementioned 
deeply-mixed boundary layer will cause most of that precipitation to 
sublimate/evaporate to virga, a few sprinkles will be possible 
especially over the ne Piedmont and nrn-cntl Coastal Plain in the 
several hours centered around sunset Fri. 

That reinforcing front will otherwise usher even chillier and drier 
air across cntl NC for the weekend. Point forecast soundings 
continue to depict relatively steep low-level lapse rates in CAA 
behind it Fri night, which may include a potential for gustiness 
between 20-30 kts as a surge of nwly momentum in the residual mixed 
layer arrives during the evening. While related mixing should 
gradually weaken through Sat morning, it will hinder further 
cooling potential via radiative processes. As such, the coldest 
temperatures are expected when the CAA wanes and the MSL pressure 
gradient relaxes by Sun and Mon morning, when sub-freezing 
temperatures appear likely and a hard freeze will be possible 
especially in outlying/rural Piedmont locations. 

While dewpoints and relative humidity values have been adjusted 
lower than both the previous forecast and the latest NBM (with its 
systematic high bias), forecast minimum RH for both Fri and Sat are 
mostly between 30-40%. Although those values may continue to trend 
lower and nearer IFD criteria (25-30%), the greater mitigating 
parameters for increased fire danger will be wind/gusts, given only 
teens kts momentum transfer indicated in the mixed layer both days, 
and cool temperatures in the 50s.  

While some moderation will result as the high gradually weakens and 
airmass modifies through most of next week, its continued presence 
and influence will yield continued below average temperatures and 
multiple, consecutive mornings of frost/freeze conditions.
